## Why This Is Asked
Tests understanding of open/closed principles, plugin registries, and runtime configurability for cross-cutting concerns like logging.

## Key Concepts
- Strategy pattern
- Registry / plugin architecture
- Thread-safety and dynamic configuration
- Separation of concerns in logging

## Code Example
```javascript
interface LogEvent { level: string; message: string; ts: number; }
interface LogFormatter { format(event: LogEvent): string; }
class JSONFormatter implements LogFormatter { format(e: LogEvent) { return JSON.stringify(e); } }
class KVFormatter implements LogFormatter { format(e: LogEvent) { return `ts=${e.ts} level=${e.level} msg='${e.message}'`; } }
class Registry<T> { private map = new Map<string, T>(); register(name: string, v: T){ this.map.set(name, v); } get(name: string): T | undefined { return this.map.get(name); } }
```

## Follow-up Questions
- How would you handle thread-safety in a multi-threaded environment?
- How to test registering and switching formatters in isolation?

## Why This Is Asked
This question probes real-world extensibility: adding rules without redeploying, and per-message routing based on metadata.

## Key Concepts
- Runtime plugin architecture with a Registry

- How would you handle rule versioning and rollback?
- What are the trade-offs of eager vs lazy loading of rules?

## Why This Is Asked

- How would you test the registry and routing guarantees?
- What metrics would you collect for backpressure and throughput?

## Why This Is Asked
Beginner-friendly exploration of extensibility and non-blocking I/O: add new sinks without changing core, and isolate failures per sink.

## Key Concepts
- Strategy/Plug-in pattern for runtime extension
- Registry mapping names to Sink implementations
- Non-blocking writes via per-sink queuing and worker pool
- Fault isolation and graceful degradation

## Code Example
```typescript
interface Sink { write(msg: string): Promise<void> }
class Registry { addSink(name: string, s: Sink): void; getSinks(): Sink[] }
class Logger { constructor(private reg: Registry) ; log(msg: string): void { for (const s of reg.getSinks()) s.write(msg); } }
```

## Follow-up Questions
- How would you test sink isolation and backpressure?
- How would you implement graceful shutdown for all sinks?

## Why This Is Asked
Shows how to design pluggable, runtime-extendable policy logic for high-stakes API gateways while avoiding restarts. Tests hot-swap safety and ordering guarantees.

## Key Concepts
- Strategy + Registry for dynamic rule loading
- Short-circuit evaluation and backpressure of policy decisions
- Atomic swaps for hot-reload without downtime

## Code Example
```javascript
interface Rule { apply(req: Request): { ok: boolean; reason?: string } }
class Registry { register(name: string, factory: ()=>Rule); create(name: string, ...args:any[]): Rule }
class PolicyPipeline { addRule(name: string, args?: any): void; evaluate(req: Request): { ok: boolean; reason?: string } }
```

## Follow-up Questions
- How would you handle rule dependencies and initialization order?
- How would you test hot-reload without affecting live traffic?
